weeks.lessonTitle: Vowel Sounds /e/ and /æ/, Pronouns (Personal, Possessive, Reflexive), Informal & Formal Letters, and Oral vs Written Literature
weeks.content:
Vowel /e/ is a short front vowel heard in "bed", "pen", "head", "many", "said", "bury", and "leopard". Vowel /æ/ is a short front open vowel heard in "cat", "man", "bag", "plait", and "hand".
Pronouns replace nouns to avoid repetition. Personal pronouns have subjective case (I, we, he, she, they) and objective case (me, us, him, her, them).

12. Which of the following words contains the short vowel sound /e/ as in "bed"?
- A) Leopard
- B) Plait
- C) Heart
- D) Bead
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: In "leopard" (/ˈlepəd/), the "eo" spelling is pronounced with the short vowel /e/.

13. Which word has the same vowel sound /æ/ as the vowel in "pack"?
- A) Plait
- B) Park
- C) Peck
- D) Peak
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: "Plait" (/plæt/) is pronounced with the short vowel /æ/, matching "pack" (/pæk/).

14. Select the grammatically correct pronoun to complete the sentence: "The Principal commended Tunde and _____ for tidying the library."
- A) I
- B) me
- C) myself
- D) mine
Correct Answer: B
Explanation: The pronoun is the direct object of the transitive verb "commended", so the objective case "me" is required.

15. How many addresses appear in a standard Informal Letter compared to a Formal (Official) Letter?
- A) One writer's address in an informal letter; two addresses (writer's and recipient's) in a formal letter
- B) Two addresses in an informal letter; one address in a formal letter
- C) Two addresses in both informal and formal letters
- D) No address in an informal letter; one address in a formal letter
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: An informal letter has only the writer's address and date at the top right, whereas a formal letter has both the writer's address and the recipient's official address.

16. Which of the following is an example of Oral Literature (Orature) transmitted by word of mouth before written print?
- A) Folktales, proverbs, riddles, and panegyric praise chants
- B) Printed encyclopedias and newspaper editorials
- C) Autobiographies published in hardcover volumes
- D) Stage screenplays printed with ISBN numbers
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Folktales, myths, legends, proverbs, riddles, and traditional praise chants belong to oral literature.

weeks.content:
Vowel /ɑ:/ is a long back vowel heard in "car", "father", "part", "heart", "calm", "palm", "clerk", and "laugh". Vowel /ɒ/ is a short back vowel heard in "pot", "hot", "dog", "what", "watch", "want", and "cough".
A transitive verb takes a direct object (e.g., "Ada kicked the ball"), whereas an intransitive verb does not take a direct object (e.g., "The baby slept peacefully").

17. Which of the following words contains the long vowel sound /ɑ:/ as in "father"?
- A) Heart
- B) What
- C) Hat
- D) Hurt
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: "Heart" (/hɑːt/) contains the long back vowel /ɑ:/, whereas "what" has /ɒ/, "hat" has /æ/, and "hurt" has /ɜ:/.

18. Which of the following words contains the short vowel sound /ɒ/ as in "pot"?
- A) Watch
- B) Water
- C)Word
- D) Warm
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: "Watch" (/wɒtʃ/) contains the short vowel /ɒ/, whereas "water" and "warm" contain /ɔ:/ and "word" contains /ɜ:/.

19. In which of the following sentences is the underlined verb used INTRANSITIVELY?
- A) The choir sang a melodious anthem during assembly.
- B) The guests arrived early at the reception hall.
- C) The carpenter repaired the broken wooden desk.
- D) Our captain lifted the championship trophy.
Correct Answer: B
Explanation: In "The guests arrived early at the reception hall," the verb "arrived" has no direct object ("early" and "at the reception hall" are adverbials), making it intransitive.

20. What distinguishes a Myth from a Legend in oral literature?
- A) A myth explains supernatural origins, creation, and deities, whereas a legend is rooted in historical heroes and events with exaggerated exploits
- B) A myth is a modern newspaper report, whereas a legend is a scientific laboratory manual
- C) A myth is always acted on stage, whereas a legend is always written in rhyming couplets
- D) A myth deals only with farm animals, whereas a legend deals only with plants
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Myths explain cosmic origins, gods, and supernatural phenomena, while legends center on historical figures or heroes whose deeds are magnified over time.

- A) Bought
- B) Book
- C) Boat

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: "He fought like a lion" is a simile, whereas "He was a lion in battle" is a metaphor.

30. In the sentence "The students listened attentively in the auditorium yesterday," which types of adverbs are "attentively", "in the auditorium", and "yesterday"?
- A) Adverb of manner, adverbial of place, and adverb of time
- B) Adverb of frequency, adverb of degree, and adverb of reason
- C) Adverb of time, adverb of manner, and adverb of place
- D) Adverb of concession, adverb of purpose, and adverb of frequency
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: "Attentively" tells how (manner), "in the auditorium" tells where (place), and "yesterday" tells when (time).

weeks.detectedHeading: Week 7: Mid-Term Review & Vowel Sounds /ɜ:/ and /ə/ (The Schwa Sound)
weeks.lessonTitle: Mid-Term Review & Vowel Sounds /ɜ:/ and /ə/ (The Schwa Sound)
weeks.content:
Vowel /ɜ:/ is a long central vowel heard in "bird", "girl", "first", "shirt", "work", "word", "world", "nurse", "church", "learn", "earth", and "journey".
Vowel /ə/ (the schwa sound) is the shortest, weakest central vowel occurring in unstressed syllables such as "about", "teacher", "doctor", "father", "ago", and "police".

31. Which of the following words contains the long central vowel sound /ɜ:/ as in "bird"?
- A) Journey
- B) Morning
- C) Heart
- D) Beard
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: "Journey" (/ˈdʒɜːni/) contains the long central vowel /ɜ:/, just like "bird", "work", and "learn".

32. Which pure vowel sound is known as the "schwa" and occurs only in unstressed syllables such as the first syllable of "about" (/əˈbaʊt/) and the last syllable of "teacher" (/ˈtiːtʃə/)?
- A) /ə/
- B) /ɜ:/
- C) /ʌ/
- D) /æ/
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: The schwa (/ə/) is the weak, unstressed central vowel sound in English phonology.

33. Which of the following pairs of words both contain the vowel sound /ɜ:/?
- A) Nurse and World
- B) Course and Court
- C) Heart and Herd
- D) Pour and Pure
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Both "nurse" (/nɜːs/) and "world" (/wɜːld/) contain the long central vowel /ɜ:/.

weeks.detectedHeading: Week 8: Prepositions, Conjunctions, and Interjections
weeks.lessonTitle: Prepositions, Conjunctions, and Interjections
weeks.content:
A preposition shows the relationship in space, time, or direction between a noun/pronoun and another word in a sentence (e.g., in, on, at, between, among, beside, besides, since, for).
Conjunctions join words, phrases, or clauses and include coordinating conjunctions (FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so), correlative conjunctions (either...or, neither...nor, both...and, not only...but also), and subordinating conjunctions (because, although, unless, while).

34. Complete the sentence accurately: "The prize money was shared equally _____ the two debaters, whereas the certificates were distributed _____ all forty students in the class."
- A) between / among
- B) among / between
- C) beside / besides
- D) within / between
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: "Between" is used for two persons or items, whereas "among" is used for three or more.

35. Choose the correct correlative conjunction pair to complete the sentence: "_____ the class captain _____ his assistant was present when the bell rang."
- A) Neither / nor
- B) Neither / or
- C) Either / nor
- D) Both / or
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: "Neither" pairs strictly with "nor" ("Neither...nor"), and with singular subjects the verb agrees with the nearer singular subject ("was").

36. Complete the sentence with the correct time prepositions: "Mrs. Okafor has taught in this school _____ 2019, which means she has taught here _____ seven years."
- A) since / for
- B) for / since
- C) from / since
- D) during / from
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: "Since" marks a specific starting point in time (2019), while "for" marks a duration or period of time (seven years).

weeks.detectedHeading: Week 9: Formal Letter Writing, Reading Comprehension Strategies, and Prose Elements (Plot, Setting, Characterization, Theme)
weeks.lessonTitle: Formal Letter Writing, Reading Comprehension Strategies, and Prose Elements (Plot, Setting, Characterization, Theme)
weeks.content:
A formal letter is written for official purposes (to a Principal, Commissioner, Editor, or Manager). It features two addresses, a formal salutation ("Dear Sir," or "Dear Madam,"), a clear underlined/capitalized title, formal tone without contractions or slang, and closes with "Yours faithfully," followed by signature and full name.

37. Which combination of Salutation and Subscription (complimentary close) is strictly required in a standard Formal Letter addressed to an official whose name is not used in the salutation?
- A) Dear Sir, / Yours faithfully,
- B) Dear Uncle, / Yours sincerely,
- C) Hello Sir, / Yours truly,
- D) Dear Mr. President, / Yours affectionately,
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: A formal letter opening with "Dear Sir," or "Dear Madam," must close with "Yours faithfully," followed by the writer's signature and full name.

38. Which of the following features is strictly FORBIDDEN in a Formal Letter?
- A) Contracted verb forms (such as "don't", "can't"), slang, and colloquial jokes
- B) The recipient's official designation and address on the left-hand side
- C) A concise subject heading summarizing the purpose of the letter
- D) The writer's signature above the writer's full name at the end
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Formal letters require an objective, polite, official register and forbid contractions, slang, or chatty pleasantries.

39. In prose literature, what term refers to the central underlying message or universal truth explored by the author throughout the work?
- A) Theme
- B) Setting
- C) Prologue
- D) Diction
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: The theme is the central idea, moral insight, or underlying message of a literary work, while setting refers to the time and place of events.

weeks.detectedHeading: Week 10: Revision of Tenses (Simple Present, Present Continuous, Simple Past, Present Perfect) and Figures of Speech (Hyperbole, Irony, Onomatopoeia, Oxymoron)
weeks.lessonTitle: Revision of Tenses (Simple Present, Present Continuous, Simple Past, Present Perfect) and Figures of Speech (Hyperbole, Irony, Onomatopoeia, Oxymoron)
weeks.content:
The simple present tense expresses habitual actions and universal truths ("Water boils at $100^\circ\text{C}$"). The simple past expresses completed actions at a definite past time ("She visited Kano last week").
Onomatopoeia uses words whose sounds suggest their meaning (buzz, hiss, splash, tick-tock); Oxymoron places two contradictory words side by side ("bittersweet", "open secret", "deafening silence").

40. Identify the figure of speech in the expression: "There was a deafening silence in the examination hall when the papers were distributed."
- A) Oxymoron
- B) Simile
- C) Personification
- D) Assonance
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Placing two contrasting words ("deafening" and "silence") side by side for poetic effect is an oxymoron.

41. Identify the figure of speech in the sentence: "I have told you a million times not to leave your textbook in the rain."
- A) Hyperbole
- B) Litotes
- C) Metonymy
- D) Pun
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: "A million times" is a deliberate exaggeration for emphasis, which is hyperbole.

42. Choose the correct verb form to complete the sentence expressing a scientific truth: "The Earth _____ around the Sun once every year."
- A) revolves
- B) revolved
- C) is revolving
- D) has been revolved
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Universal truths and permanent natural laws take the simple present tense ("revolves").

documents.title: JSS 1 Basic Science — St. Francis Catholic Secondary School First Term (Weeks 1–11)
documents.subject: Basic Science
documents.description: St. Francis Catholic Secondary School Lagos JSS 1 Basic Science First Term Note covering Matter & States of Matter, Living & Non-Living Things, Plant & Animal Cells, Metals & Non-Metals, Human Development & Puberty, Sanitation, Nutrition & Balanced Diet, Drug Abuse, Reproductive System, and STIs / HIV/AIDS (Weeks 1–11).
documents.rawText:
[Page 1]
Week 1: Living and Non-Living Things I — Meaning, Identification, and States of Matter
Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. Matter exists in three primary physical states: solid, liquid, and gas.
Solids have a definite shape and definite volume with tightly packed particles vibrating in fixed positions. Liquids have a definite volume but take the shape of their container. Gases have neither a definite shape nor a definite volume and are highly compressible.
Phase transitions include melting (solid to liquid), freezing (liquid to solid), evaporation/boiling (liquid to gas), condensation (gas to liquid), and sublimation (solid directly to gas, as in camphor, iodine crystals, and ammonium chloride).

1. What phase transition occurs when solid iodine crystals or camphor change directly into gaseous vapour upon heating without passing through the liquid state?
- A) Sublimation
- B) Condensation
- C) Evaporation
- D) Fusion
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Sublimation is the direct transition of a substance from the solid state to the gaseous state without becoming a liquid.

2. Why does a gas completely fill any container into which it is placed and remain easily compressible?
- A) Its particles are far apart with negligible intermolecular forces of attraction and move randomly at high speeds
- B) Its particles are locked in rigid crystal lattices with strong cohesive bonds
- C) Its particles have fixed volume and slide slowly over one another at the bottom of the vessel
- D) Its particles expand in mass whenever the container temperature drops
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Gas particles have very weak intermolecular forces and wide spaces between them, allowing rapid random motion and easy compression.

3. What is the fundamental difference between the mass and the weight of a body?
- A) Mass is the constant quantity of matter in a body measured in kilograms ($\text{kg}$), whereas weight is the gravitational pull on the body measured in Newtons ($\text{N}$) and varies from place to place
- B) Mass is measured in Newtons using a spring balance, whereas weight is measured in kilograms using a beam balance
- C) Mass varies with altitude and gravity, whereas weight remains constant throughout the universe
- D) Mass is a vector force directed downward, whereas weight is a scalar measure of volume
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Mass ($\text{kg}$) is constant everywhere, while weight ($W = mg$, in Newtons) depends on local gravitational acceleration.

4. Which of the following processes releases heat energy as gaseous water vapour turns back into liquid droplets on a cold surface?
- A) Condensation
- B) Melting
- C) Sublimation
- D) Boiling
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Condensation is the change of state from gas (vapour) to liquid when cooled.

[Page 3]
Week 2: Living and Non-Living Things II — Characteristics of Living Things (MR NIGER D) and Classification of Living Things
Living things carry out core life processes summarized by MR NIGER D: Movement (locomotion or growth curvature), Respiration (breakdown of glucose to release energy), Nutrition (autotrophic in green plants; heterotrophic in animals), Irritability/Sensitivity (response to external stimuli), Growth (irreversible increase in size and dry mass), Excretion (removal of toxic metabolic waste products), Reproduction, and Death.

5. Which life process involves the chemical breakdown of food substances (glucose) inside living cells to release energy for metabolic activities?
- A) Respiration
- B) Excretion
- C) Egestion
- D) Transpiration
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Cellular respiration breaks down glucose to release usable energy (ATP), whereas breathing is merely gaseous exchange.

6. Why is the removal of undigested food faeces through the anus called egestion rather than excretion?
- A) Undigested faeces were never absorbed into body cells or formed by cellular metabolism, whereas excretion removes metabolic waste like urea, sweat, and carbon dioxide
- B) Egestion occurs only in green plants, whereas excretion occurs only in vertebrates
- C) Egestion takes place in the kidneys and lungs, whereas excretion takes place in the large intestine
- D) Egestion produces metabolic energy, whereas excretion stores excess glucose
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Excretion is strictly the removal of toxic waste products of cellular metabolism (urea, $\text{CO}_2$, excess salts), whereas egestion expels undigested food residue.

7. How does nutrition in green plants (autotrophic nutrition) differ fundamentally from nutrition in animals (heterotrophic nutrition)?
- A) Green plants manufacture their own organic food from carbon dioxide and water using sunlight and chlorophyll, whereas animals depend on ready-made organic food
- B) Green plants feed only on dead decaying animals, whereas animals synthesize starch in chloroplasts
- C) Green plants respire only during the day, whereas animals photosynthesize at night
- D) Green plants lack cellular membranes, whereas animals possess rigid cellulose cell walls
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Green plants are autotrophs that carry out photosynthesis using chlorophyll and sunlight, while animals are heterotrophs.

[Page 6]
Week 3: Living and Non-Living Things III — Plant and Animal Cells, Organelles, and Differences Between Plants and Animals
The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of all living organisms.
The nucleus controls all cellular activities and contains chromosomes (hereditary DNA). The mitochondrion is the "powerhouse" of the cell where aerobic respiration produces energy. The chloroplast contains green chlorophyll for photosynthesis in plant cells. The cellulose cell wall surrounds the plasma membrane in plant cells, providing rigidity and definite shape.

8. Which two structures are present in a typical green leaf palisade cell (plant cell) but completely absent in a human cheek cell (animal cell)?
- A) Rigid cellulose cell wall and chloroplasts
- B) Nucleus and selectively permeable cell membrane
- C) Mitochondria and cytoplasm
- D) Ribosomes and nuclear membrane
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Plant cells possess a rigid cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts, and a large permanent central vacuole, which animal cells lack.

9. Which cell organelle is known as the "powerhouse of the cell" because it serves as the site of cellular respiration and energy (ATP) generation?
- A) Mitochondrion
- B) Chloroplast
- C) Golgi apparatus
- D) Vacuole
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Mitochondria carry out aerobic cellular respiration to generate ATP energy for the cell.

10. In what chemical form do green plants store excess carbohydrates compared to the storage form in animals and fungi?
- A) Plants store carbohydrates as insoluble starch granules, whereas animals store carbohydrates as glycogen in the liver and muscles
- B) Plants store carbohydrates as glycogen, whereas animals store carbohydrates as cellulose
- C) Plants store carbohydrates as urea, whereas animals store carbohydrates as chlorophyll
- D) Both plants and animals store carbohydrates exclusively as sucrose crystals
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Plants store excess glucose as starch, whereas animals store excess glucose as glycogen.

[Page 9]
Week 4: Living and Non-Living Things IV — Classification of Non-Living Things into Metals and Non-Metals
Non-living elements are classified into metals (such as iron, copper, aluminium, gold, silver, zinc, sodium, calcium) and non-metals (such as oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur, carbon, chlorine, phosphorus).
Metals are lustrous (shiny), malleable (can be beaten into sheets), ductile (can be drawn into wires), sonorous, have high density and high melting points, and are good conductors of heat and electricity. During chemical reactions, metals lose electrons to form positively charged ions (cations), whereas non-metals gain or share electrons to form negatively charged ions (anions).

11. Which physical property of copper and aluminium enables them to be drawn into long, thin electrical transmission wires without snapping?
- A) Ductility
- B) Malleability
- C) Sonorousness
- D) Brittleness
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Ductility is the ability of a metal to be drawn out into thin wires, whereas malleability is the ability to be hammered or rolled into thin sheets.

12. Which of the following pairs correctly identifies a metal and a non-metal that exist as liquids at ordinary room temperature ($25^\circ\text{C}$)?
- A) Mercury (liquid metal) and Bromine (liquid non-metal)
- B) Iron (liquid metal) and Sulphur (liquid non-metal)
- C) Copper (liquid metal) and Carbon (liquid non-metal)
- D) Aluminium (liquid metal) and Iodine (liquid non-metal)
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature, and bromine is the only non-metal that is liquid at room temperature.

13. How do metal atoms and non-metal atoms behave differently with respect to valence electrons during ionic chemical reactions?
- A) Metal atoms lose electrons to form positively charged cations, whereas non-metal atoms gain electrons to form negatively charged anions
- B) Metal atoms gain electrons to form negative anions, whereas non-metal atoms lose electrons to form positive cations
- C) Both metal and non-metal atoms lose protons from their atomic nuclei
- D) Metal atoms share neutrons, whereas non-metal atoms destroy valence shells
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Metals are electropositive (losing electrons to form cations), whereas non-metals are electronegative (gaining electrons to form anions).

14. Which atypical form of the non-metal carbon is a good conductor of electricity and is used as electrodes in dry cells?
- A) Graphite
- B) Diamond
- C) Sulphur
- D) Phosphorus
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Although non-metals are generally poor conductors of electricity, graphite (an allotrope of carbon) conducts electricity due to delocalized electrons.

[Page 11]
Week 5: Human Development — Growth, Developmental Changes, and Puberty in Boys and Girls
Growth is a permanent, irreversible increase in size, height, and dry mass, whereas development is the progressive qualitative maturation of body organs, skills, and complexity.
Puberty is the stage of developmental transition from childhood to sexual maturity (adolescence), controlled by sex hormones: testosterone in boys (secreted by the testes) and oestrogen/progesterone in girls (secreted by the ovaries).

15. Which hormone is secreted by the testes to trigger secondary sexual characteristics such as deepening of the voice and facial hair growth in boys at puberty?
- A) Testosterone
- B) Oestrogen
- C) Progesterone
- D) Insulin
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Testosterone is the male androgen hormone produced by the testes during puberty.

16. Which of the following developmental changes at puberty occurs in BOTH boys and girls?
- A) Growth of pubic and armpit (axillary) hair and increased activity of sweat and sebaceous glands
- B) Onset of monthly menstruation (menarche) and widening of the pelvic girdle
- C) Enlargement of the larynx (Adam's apple) and production of sperm cells
- D) Development of mammary glands (breasts) and ovulation
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Growth of pubic and axillary hair and increased sweat/oil gland activity occur in both sexes during puberty.

17. Which statement accurately distinguishes temporary changes from permanent changes in human development?
- A) Sweating, pimples, and temporary weight fluctuations are reversible temporary changes, whereas growth in skeletal height and transition from infancy to adulthood are irreversible permanent changes
- B) Growing taller from childhood to adulthood is a temporary change, whereas sweating after exercise is a permanent change
- C) Chameleon skin colour change is a permanent change, whereas greying of hair in old age is a temporary change
- D) Both skeletal height growth and emotional moods are easily reversed at will
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Temporary changes (like sweating, hunger, or goosebumps) are reversible, whereas developmental growth and aging are permanent.

[Page 13]
Week 6: Family Health I — Personal Cleanliness, Environmental Sanitation, Refuse Disposal, and Sewage Disposal
Sanitation is the science and practice of maintaining hygienic conditions through safe disposal of refuse (solid dry waste) and sewage (liquid waste containing human excreta and wastewater).
Methods of refuse disposal include covered dustbins, incineration (burning in an incinerator), composting (converting biodegradable waste into humus manure), and sanitary landfill. Methods of sewage disposal include the water closet (WC) connected to a septic tank/soakaway pit and the pit latrine.

18. What is the precise distinction between "refuse" and "sewage" in environmental sanitation?
- A) Refuse consists of solid dry waste materials (such as paper, tins, plastics, and food peels), whereas sewage consists of liquid wastewater and human excreta (urine and faeces)
- B) Refuse is flushed through underground water pipes, whereas sewage is burned in open incinerators
- C) Refuse contains only liquid industrial chemicals, whereas sewage contains only dry fallen leaves
- D) Refuse is disposed of in septic tanks, whereas sewage is recycled into plastic bottles
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Refuse is solid waste, while sewage is liquid waste containing human excreta and domestic/industrial wastewater.

19. Which method of refuse disposal decomposes biodegradable organic waste (such as vegetable peels and plant leaves) through microbial action to produce nutrient-rich farm manure?
- A) Composting
- B) Incineration
- C) Open dumping
- D) Pulverization of plastics
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Composting biologically decomposes organic biodegradable refuse into rich humus fertilizer.

20. Why must non-biodegradable refuse such as plastic bottles, polythene bags, and glass jars be separated from compost pits?
- A) Microorganisms cannot decompose non-biodegradable materials, so they persist in soil and cause long-term land pollution
- B) Non-biodegradable plastics dissolve instantly in rainwater to form nitrogen fertilizer
- C) Non-biodegradable glass evaporates into the atmosphere at room temperature
- D) Soil earthworms consume glass and polythene as their primary source of protein
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Non-biodegradable materials cannot be broken down by natural decomposers (bacteria and fungi) and must be recycled or reused instead.

[Page 16]
Week 8: Family Health II — Nutrition, Classes of Food, and Balanced Diet
Nutrition is the process of taking in and utilizing food substances for energy, growth, tissue repair, and protection against disease.
The six classes of food are: Carbohydrates (glucose, yam, rice, bread — primary source of energy), Proteins (beans, fish, meat, egg, milk — growth and repair of worn-out tissues; deficiency causes Kwashiorkor), Fats and Oils (palm oil, butter, groundnut — concentrated energy and thermal insulation), Vitamins (organic protective nutrients; Vitamin A prevents night blindness, Vitamin C prevents scurvy, Vitamin D prevents rickets, Vitamin K aids blood clotting), Mineral Salts (calcium and phosphorus for bones/teeth, iron for haemoglobin, iodine to prevent goitre), and Water.

21. A young child fed almost exclusively on starchy pap and cassava develops a swollen pot-belly, thin wasted limbs, oedema, and reddish-brown scanty hair. Which nutritional deficiency disease is this?
- A) Kwashiorkor (severe protein deficiency)
- B) Scurvy (Vitamin C deficiency)
- C) Goitre (Iodine deficiency)
- D) Rickets (Vitamin D and Calcium deficiency)
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Kwashiorkor is caused by severe protein deficiency in children whose diet consists almost entirely of starchy carbohydrates.

22. Which pair correctly matches a specific vitamin with the deficiency condition caused by its absence in the human diet?
- A) Vitamin C — Scurvy (bleeding gums and poor wound healing); Vitamin D — Rickets (soft, bowed bones)
- B) Vitamin A — Beriberi; Vitamin K — Night blindness
- C) Vitamin B1 — Rickets; Vitamin C — Failure of blood to clot
- D) Vitamin D — Bleeding gums; Vitamin A — Goitre
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness, Vitamin B1 causes beriberi, Vitamin C causes scurvy, Vitamin D causes rickets, and Vitamin K causes defective blood clotting.

23. Which mineral element is an essential component of haemoglobin in red blood cells, and which mineral element prevents enlargement of the thyroid gland (goitre)?
- A) Iron (for haemoglobin) and Iodine (to prevent goitre)
- B) Sodium (for haemoglobin) and Potassium (to prevent goitre)
- C) Calcium (for haemoglobin) and Fluorine (to prevent goitre)
- D) Magnesium (for haemoglobin) and Chlorine (to prevent goitre)
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Iron is required to synthesize oxygen-carrying haemoglobin (deficiency causes anaemia), while iodine is required by the thyroid gland to synthesize thyroxine (deficiency causes goitre).

24. Which chemical reagents are used in the laboratory to test for the presence of Starch and Simple Reducing Sugar (Glucose) respectively?
- A) Iodine solution (turns blue-black with starch) and Fehling's or Benedict's solution (turns brick-red precipitate on heating with glucose)
- B) Million's reagent (for starch) and Sudan III solution (for glucose)
- C) Litmus paper (for starch) and limewater (for glucose)
- D) Biuret reagent (for starch) and translucent paper mark (for glucose)
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Iodine solution turns blue-black with starch; Fehling's/Benedict's solution gives a brick-red precipitate with reducing sugars; Biuret/Millon's tests for protein; Sudan III/translucent spot tests for fats and oils.

[Page 19]
Week 9: Family Health III — Drug and Substance Abuse
A drug is any chemical substance other than food that alters the physiological or psychological functioning of the body when taken.
Drug abuse is the use of a drug without a qualified doctor's prescription, taking an overdose/underdose, or using prohibited narcotics and stimulants (such as cocaine, heroin, cannabis/marijuana, tramadol abuse, and alcohol). In Nigeria, NAFDAC regulates food and drug safety while NDLEA enforces laws against illicit drug trafficking and abuse.

25. Which of the following practices constitutes drug abuse even when using a legal pharmaceutical medicine?
- A) Self-medicating with antibiotics without a doctor's prescription or stopping the dosage before completing the prescribed course
- B) Taking the exact dosage of antimalarial tablets prescribed by a licensed physician at the recommended intervals
- C) Checking the NAFDAC registration number and expiry date before purchasing a medicine from a registered pharmacy
- D) Storing prescribed liquid medicines out of the reach of toddlers as instructed by a pharmacist
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Self-medication, sharing prescriptions, taking overdoses, or failing to complete prescribed antibiotic courses are forms of drug misuse/abuse.

26. In Nigeria, which two federal agencies are respectively responsible for (i) regulating the manufacture and safety of food, drugs, and cosmetics, and (ii) combating illicit hard drug trafficking and abuse?
- A) NAFDAC and NDLEA
- B) FRSC and NEMA
- C) INEC and EFCC
- D) SON and ICPC
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: NAFDAC (National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control) regulates food/drug quality, while NDLEA (National Drug Law Enforcement Agency) combats illicit narcotics.

[Page 22]
Week 10: Reproductive System — Male and Female Reproductive Organs and Fertilization
The male reproductive system includes the testes (held in the scrotal sac to maintain a temperature slightly below body temperature for sperm production), epididymis, vas deferens (sperm duct), seminal vesicles, prostate gland, and penis/urethra.
The female reproductive system includes the ovaries (produce ova/eggs and female sex hormones), fallopian tubes/oviducts (the exact site where fertilization occurs), uterus/womb (where the implanted embryo/foetus develops), cervix, and vagina (birth canal).

27. In which specific organ of the human female reproductive system does fertilization (fusion of the male sperm nucleus and female ovum nucleus) normally take place?
- A) Fallopian tube (oviduct)
- B) Uterus (womb)
- C) Ovary
- D) Cervix
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Fertilization takes place in the upper part of the fallopian tube (oviduct), after which the zygote travels to the uterus for implantation.

28. Why are the human testes suspended outside the abdominal cavity inside the scrotal sac?
- A) Healthy sperm production (spermatogenesis) requires a temperature $2^\circ\text{C}$ to $3^\circ\text{C}$ lower than normal core body temperature ($37^\circ\text{C}$)
- B) The abdominal cavity lacks blood vessels to supply oxygen to the testes
- C) The scrotal sac heats the testes to $42^\circ\text{C}$ to accelerate hormone breakdown
- D) Sperm cells are produced in the kidneys and only pass through the scrotum during urination
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: The scrotum keeps the testes slightly cooler than core body temperature ($37^\circ\text{C}$), which is essential for viable sperm production.

[Page 24]
Week 11: Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs), HIV/AIDS, Modes of Transmission, and Prevention
Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) include gonorrhoea, syphilis, chlamydia, genital herpes, trichomoniasis, and HIV/AIDS.
HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) attacks and destroys the body's CD4 white blood cells (helper T-lymphocytes), weakening the immune system and leading to AIDS (Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome). HIV is transmitted through unprotected sexual intercourse, transfusion of unscreened infected blood, sharing unsterilized sharp instruments (needles, blades, clippers), and mother-to-child transmission during pregnancy, childbirth, or breastfeeding. HIV is NOT transmitted by mosquito bites, shaking hands, hugging, or sharing plates.

29. How does the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) cause Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS) in an infected person?
- A) It progressively attacks and destroys the body's CD4 helper T-lymphocytes (white blood cells), leaving the body defenseless against opportunistic infections
- B) It multiplies inside red blood cells to increase oxygen transport in the bloodstream
- C) It strengthens bone marrow platelets so that blood clots inside the digestive tract
- D) It converts liver glycogen into excess insulin within twenty-four hours of exposure
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: HIV destroys CD4 white blood cells of the immune system, making the patient vulnerable to opportunistic infections.

30. Which of the following CANNOT transmit HIV from an infected person to a healthy person?
- A) Sharing classroom desks, shaking hands, hugging, or being bitten by mosquitoes
- B) Receiving a blood transfusion of unscreened HIV-positive blood
- C) Sharing unsterilized hypodermic needles, razor blades, or tattooing instruments
- D) Mother-to-child transmission during childbirth or breastfeeding without antiretroviral care
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Casual contact (shaking hands, hugging, sharing seats/utensils) and insect bites do not transmit HIV.

weeks.detectedHeading: Week 1: Living and Non-Living Things I — Meaning, Identification, and States of Matter
weeks.lessonTitle: Living and Non-Living Things I — Meaning, Identification, and States of Matter
weeks.content:
Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. Matter exists in three primary physical states: solid, liquid, and gas.
Solids have a definite shape and definite volume with tightly packed particles vibrating in fixed positions. Liquids have a definite volume but take the shape of their container. Gases have neither a definite shape nor a definite volume and are highly compressible.
Phase transitions include melting (solid to liquid), freezing (liquid to solid), evaporation/boiling (liquid to gas), condensation (gas to liquid), and sublimation (solid directly to gas, as in camphor, iodine crystals, and ammonium chloride).

1. What phase transition occurs when solid iodine crystals or camphor change directly into gaseous vapour upon heating without passing through the liquid state?
- A) Sublimation
- B) Condensation
- C) Evaporation
- D) Fusion
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Sublimation is the direct transition of a substance from the solid state to the gaseous state without becoming a liquid.

2. Why does a gas completely fill any container into which it is placed and remain easily compressible?
- A) Its particles are far apart with negligible intermolecular forces of attraction and move randomly at high speeds
- B) Its particles are locked in rigid crystal lattices with strong cohesive bonds
- C) Its particles have fixed volume and slide slowly over one another at the bottom of the vessel
- D) Its particles expand in mass whenever the container temperature drops
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Gas particles have very weak intermolecular forces and wide spaces between them, allowing rapid random motion and easy compression.

3. What is the fundamental difference between the mass and the weight of a body?
- A) Mass is the constant quantity of matter in a body measured in kilograms ($\text{kg}$), whereas weight is the gravitational pull on the body measured in Newtons ($\text{N}$) and varies from place to place
- B) Mass is measured in Newtons using a spring balance, whereas weight is measured in kilograms using a beam balance
- C) Mass varies with altitude and gravity, whereas weight remains constant throughout the universe
- D) Mass is a vector force directed downward, whereas weight is a scalar measure of volume
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Mass ($\text{kg}$) is constant everywhere, while weight ($W = mg$, in Newtons) depends on local gravitational acceleration.

4. Which of the following processes releases heat energy as gaseous water vapour turns back into liquid droplets on a cold surface?
- A) Condensation
- B) Melting
- C) Sublimation
- D) Boiling
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Condensation is the change of state from gas (vapour) to liquid when cooled.

weeks.detectedHeading: Week 2: Living and Non-Living Things II — Characteristics of Living Things (MR NIGER D) and Classification of Living Things
weeks.lessonTitle: Living and Non-Living Things II — Characteristics of Living Things (MR NIGER D) and Classification of Living Things
weeks.content:
Living things carry out core life processes summarized by MR NIGER D: Movement (locomotion or growth curvature), Respiration (breakdown of glucose to release energy), Nutrition (autotrophic in green plants; heterotrophic in animals), Irritability/Sensitivity (response to external stimuli), Growth (irreversible increase in size and dry mass), Excretion (removal of toxic metabolic waste products), Reproduction, and Death.

5. Which life process involves the chemical breakdown of food substances (glucose) inside living cells to release energy for metabolic activities?
- A) Respiration
- B) Excretion
- C) Egestion
- D) Transpiration
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Cellular respiration breaks down glucose to release usable energy (ATP), whereas breathing is merely gaseous exchange.

6. Why is the removal of undigested food faeces through the anus called egestion rather than excretion?
- A) Undigested faeces were never absorbed into body cells or formed by cellular metabolism, whereas excretion removes metabolic waste like urea, sweat, and carbon dioxide
- B) Egestion occurs only in green plants, whereas excretion occurs only in vertebrates
- C) Egestion takes place in the kidneys and lungs, whereas excretion takes place in the large intestine
- D) Egestion produces metabolic energy, whereas excretion stores excess glucose
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Excretion is strictly the removal of toxic waste products of cellular metabolism (urea, $\text{CO}_2$, excess salts), whereas egestion expels undigested food residue.

7. How does nutrition in green plants (autotrophic nutrition) differ fundamentally from nutrition in animals (heterotrophic nutrition)?
- A) Green plants manufacture their own organic food from carbon dioxide and water using sunlight and chlorophyll, whereas animals depend on ready-made organic food
- B) Green plants feed only on dead decaying animals, whereas animals synthesize starch in chloroplasts
- C) Green plants respire only during the day, whereas animals photosynthesize at night
- D) Green plants lack cellular membranes, whereas animals possess rigid cellulose cell walls
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Green plants are autotrophs that carry out photosynthesis using chlorophyll and sunlight, while animals are heterotrophs.

weeks.detectedHeading: Week 3: Living and Non-Living Things III — Plant and Animal Cells, Organelles, and Differences Between Plants and Animals
weeks.lessonTitle: Living and Non-Living Things III — Plant and Animal Cells, Organelles, and Differences Between Plants and Animals
weeks.content:
The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of all living organisms.
The nucleus controls all cellular activities and contains chromosomes (hereditary DNA). The mitochondrion is the "powerhouse" of the cell where aerobic respiration produces energy. The chloroplast contains green chlorophyll for photosynthesis in plant cells. The cellulose cell wall surrounds the plasma membrane in plant cells, providing rigidity and definite shape.

8. Which two structures are present in a typical green leaf palisade cell (plant cell) but completely absent in a human cheek cell (animal cell)?
- A) Rigid cellulose cell wall and chloroplasts
- B) Nucleus and selectively permeable cell membrane
- C) Mitochondria and cytoplasm
- D) Ribosomes and nuclear membrane
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Plant cells possess a rigid cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts, and a large permanent central vacuole, which animal cells lack.

9. Which cell organelle is known as the "powerhouse of the cell" because it serves as the site of cellular respiration and energy (ATP) generation?
- A) Mitochondrion
- B) Chloroplast
- C) Golgi apparatus
- D) Vacuole
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Mitochondria carry out aerobic cellular respiration to generate ATP energy for the cell.

10. In what chemical form do green plants store excess carbohydrates compared to the storage form in animals and fungi?
- A) Plants store carbohydrates as insoluble starch granules, whereas animals store carbohydrates as glycogen in the liver and muscles
- B) Plants store carbohydrates as glycogen, whereas animals store carbohydrates as cellulose
- C) Plants store carbohydrates as urea, whereas animals store carbohydrates as chlorophyll
- D) Both plants and animals store carbohydrates exclusively as sucrose crystals
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Plants store excess glucose as starch, whereas animals store excess glucose as glycogen.

weeks.detectedHeading: Week 4: Living and Non-Living Things IV — Classification of Non-Living Things into Metals and Non-Metals
weeks.lessonTitle: Living and Non-Living Things IV — Classification of Non-Living Things into Metals and Non-Metals
weeks.content:
Non-living elements are classified into metals (such as iron, copper, aluminium, gold, silver, zinc, sodium, calcium) and non-metals (such as oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur, carbon, chlorine, phosphorus).
Metals are lustrous (shiny), malleable (can be beaten into sheets), ductile (can be drawn into wires), sonorous, have high density and high melting points, and are good conductors of heat and electricity. During chemical reactions, metals lose electrons to form positively charged ions (cations), whereas non-metals gain or share electrons to form negatively charged ions (anions).

11. Which physical property of copper and aluminium enables them to be drawn into long, thin electrical transmission wires without snapping?
- A) Ductility
- B) Malleability
- C) Sonorousness
- D) Brittleness
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Ductility is the ability of a metal to be drawn out into thin wires, whereas malleability is the ability to be hammered or rolled into thin sheets.

12. Which of the following pairs correctly identifies a metal and a non-metal that exist as liquids at ordinary room temperature ($25^\circ\text{C}$)?
- A) Mercury (liquid metal) and Bromine (liquid non-metal)
- B) Iron (liquid metal) and Sulphur (liquid non-metal)
- C) Copper (liquid metal) and Carbon (liquid non-metal)
- D) Aluminium (liquid metal) and Iodine (liquid non-metal)
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature, and bromine is the only non-metal that is liquid at room temperature.

13. How do metal atoms and non-metal atoms behave differently with respect to valence electrons during ionic chemical reactions?
- A) Metal atoms lose electrons to form positively charged cations, whereas non-metal atoms gain electrons to form negatively charged anions
- B) Metal atoms gain electrons to form negative anions, whereas non-metal atoms lose electrons to form positive cations
- C) Both metal and non-metal atoms lose protons from their atomic nuclei
- D) Metal atoms share neutrons, whereas non-metal atoms destroy valence shells
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Metals are electropositive (losing electrons to form cations), whereas non-metals are electronegative (gaining electrons to form anions).

14. Which atypical form of the non-metal carbon is a good conductor of electricity and is used as electrodes in dry cells?
- A) Graphite
- B) Diamond
- C) Sulphur
- D) Phosphorus
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Although non-metals are generally poor conductors of electricity, graphite (an allotrope of carbon) conducts electricity due to delocalized electrons.

weeks.detectedHeading: Week 5: Human Development — Growth, Developmental Changes, and Puberty in Boys and Girls
weeks.lessonTitle: Human Development — Growth, Developmental Changes, and Puberty in Boys and Girls
weeks.content:
Growth is a permanent, irreversible increase in size, height, and dry mass, whereas development is the progressive qualitative maturation of body organs, skills, and complexity.
Puberty is the stage of developmental transition from childhood to sexual maturity (adolescence), controlled by sex hormones: testosterone in boys (secreted by the testes) and oestrogen/progesterone in girls (secreted by the ovaries).

15. Which hormone is secreted by the testes to trigger secondary sexual characteristics such as deepening of the voice and facial hair growth in boys at puberty?
- A) Testosterone
- B) Oestrogen
- C) Progesterone
- D) Insulin
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Testosterone is the male androgen hormone produced by the testes during puberty.

16. Which of the following developmental changes at puberty occurs in BOTH boys and girls?
- A) Growth of pubic and armpit (axillary) hair and increased activity of sweat and sebaceous glands
- B) Onset of monthly menstruation (menarche) and widening of the pelvic girdle
- C) Enlargement of the larynx (Adam's apple) and production of sperm cells
- D) Development of mammary glands (breasts) and ovulation
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Growth of pubic and axillary hair and increased sweat/oil gland activity occur in both sexes during puberty.

17. Which statement accurately distinguishes temporary changes from permanent changes in human development?
- A) Sweating, pimples, and temporary weight fluctuations are reversible temporary changes, whereas growth in skeletal height and transition from infancy to adulthood are irreversible permanent changes
- B) Growing taller from childhood to adulthood is a temporary change, whereas sweating after exercise is a permanent change
- C) Chameleon skin colour change is a permanent change, whereas greying of hair in old age is a temporary change
- D) Both skeletal height growth and emotional moods are easily reversed at will
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Temporary changes (like sweating, hunger, or goosebumps) are reversible, whereas developmental growth and aging are permanent.

weeks.detectedHeading: Week 6: Family Health I — Personal Cleanliness, Environmental Sanitation, Refuse Disposal, and Sewage Disposal
weeks.lessonTitle: Family Health I — Personal Cleanliness, Environmental Sanitation, Refuse Disposal, and Sewage Disposal
weeks.content:
Sanitation is the science and practice of maintaining hygienic conditions through safe disposal of refuse (solid dry waste) and sewage (liquid waste containing human excreta and wastewater).
Methods of refuse disposal include covered dustbins, incineration (burning in an incinerator), composting (converting biodegradable waste into humus manure), and sanitary landfill. Methods of sewage disposal include the water closet (WC) connected to a septic tank/soakaway pit and the pit latrine.

18. What is the precise distinction between "refuse" and "sewage" in environmental sanitation?
- A) Refuse consists of solid dry waste materials (such as paper, tins, plastics, and food peels), whereas sewage consists of liquid wastewater and human excreta (urine and faeces)
- B) Refuse is flushed through underground water pipes, whereas sewage is burned in open incinerators
- C) Refuse contains only liquid industrial chemicals, whereas sewage contains only dry fallen leaves
- D) Refuse is disposed of in septic tanks, whereas sewage is recycled into plastic bottles
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Refuse is solid waste, while sewage is liquid waste containing human excreta and domestic/industrial wastewater.

19. Which method of refuse disposal decomposes biodegradable organic waste (such as vegetable peels and plant leaves) through microbial action to produce nutrient-rich farm manure?
- A) Composting
- B) Incineration
- C) Open dumping
- D) Pulverization of plastics
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Composting biologically decomposes organic biodegradable refuse into rich humus fertilizer.

20. Why must non-biodegradable refuse such as plastic bottles, polythene bags, and glass jars be separated from compost pits?
- A) Microorganisms cannot decompose non-biodegradable materials, so they persist in soil and cause long-term land pollution
- B) Non-biodegradable plastics dissolve instantly in rainwater to form nitrogen fertilizer
- C) Non-biodegradable glass evaporates into the atmosphere at room temperature
- D) Soil earthworms consume glass and polythene as their primary source of protein
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Non-biodegradable materials cannot be broken down by natural decomposers (bacteria and fungi) and must be recycled or reused instead.

weeks.detectedHeading: Week 8: Family Health II — Nutrition, Classes of Food, and Balanced Diet
weeks.lessonTitle: Family Health II — Nutrition, Classes of Food, and Balanced Diet
weeks.content:
Nutrition is the process of taking in and utilizing food substances for energy, growth, tissue repair, and protection against disease.
The six classes of food are: Carbohydrates (glucose, yam, rice, bread — primary source of energy), Proteins (beans, fish, meat, egg, milk — growth and repair of worn-out tissues; deficiency causes Kwashiorkor), Fats and Oils (palm oil, butter, groundnut — concentrated energy and thermal insulation), Vitamins (organic protective nutrients; Vitamin A prevents night blindness, Vitamin C prevents scurvy, Vitamin D prevents rickets, Vitamin K aids blood clotting), Mineral Salts (calcium and phosphorus for bones/teeth, iron for haemoglobin, iodine to prevent goitre), and Water.

21. A young child fed almost exclusively on starchy pap and cassava develops a swollen pot-belly, thin wasted limbs, oedema, and reddish-brown scanty hair. Which nutritional deficiency disease is this?
- A) Kwashiorkor (severe protein deficiency)
- B) Scurvy (Vitamin C deficiency)
- C) Goitre (Iodine deficiency)
- D) Rickets (Vitamin D and Calcium deficiency)
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Kwashiorkor is caused by severe protein deficiency in children whose diet consists almost entirely of starchy carbohydrates.

22. Which pair correctly matches a specific vitamin with the deficiency condition caused by its absence in the human diet?
- A) Vitamin C — Scurvy (bleeding gums and poor wound healing); Vitamin D — Rickets (soft, bowed bones)
- B) Vitamin A — Beriberi; Vitamin K — Night blindness
- C) Vitamin B1 — Rickets; Vitamin C — Failure of blood to clot
- D) Vitamin D — Bleeding gums; Vitamin A — Goitre
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness, Vitamin B1 causes beriberi, Vitamin C causes scurvy, Vitamin D causes rickets, and Vitamin K causes defective blood clotting.

23. Which mineral element is an essential component of haemoglobin in red blood cells, and which mineral element prevents enlargement of the thyroid gland (goitre)?
- A) Iron (for haemoglobin) and Iodine (to prevent goitre)
- B) Sodium (for haemoglobin) and Potassium (to prevent goitre)
- C) Calcium (for haemoglobin) and Fluorine (to prevent goitre)
- D) Magnesium (for haemoglobin) and Chlorine (to prevent goitre)
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Iron is required to synthesize oxygen-carrying haemoglobin (deficiency causes anaemia), while iodine is required by the thyroid gland to synthesize thyroxine (deficiency causes goitre).

24. Which chemical reagents are used in the laboratory to test for the presence of Starch and Simple Reducing Sugar (Glucose) respectively?
- A) Iodine solution (turns blue-black with starch) and Fehling's or Benedict's solution (turns brick-red precipitate on heating with glucose)
- B) Million's reagent (for starch) and Sudan III solution (for glucose)
- C) Litmus paper (for starch) and limewater (for glucose)
- D) Biuret reagent (for starch) and translucent paper mark (for glucose)
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Iodine solution turns blue-black with starch; Fehling's/Benedict's solution gives a brick-red precipitate with reducing sugars; Biuret/Millon's tests for protein; Sudan III/translucent spot tests for fats and oils.

weeks.detectedHeading: Week 9: Family Health III — Drug and Substance Abuse
weeks.lessonTitle: Family Health III — Drug and Substance Abuse
weeks.content:
A drug is any chemical substance other than food that alters the physiological or psychological functioning of the body when taken.
Drug abuse is the use of a drug without a qualified doctor's prescription, taking an overdose/underdose, or using prohibited narcotics and stimulants (such as cocaine, heroin, cannabis/marijuana, tramadol abuse, and alcohol). In Nigeria, NAFDAC regulates food and drug safety while NDLEA enforces laws against illicit drug trafficking and abuse.

25. Which of the following practices constitutes drug abuse even when using a legal pharmaceutical medicine?
- A) Self-medicating with antibiotics without a doctor's prescription or stopping the dosage before completing the prescribed course
- B) Taking the exact dosage of antimalarial tablets prescribed by a licensed physician at the recommended intervals
- C) Checking the NAFDAC registration number and expiry date before purchasing a medicine from a registered pharmacy
- D) Storing prescribed liquid medicines out of the reach of toddlers as instructed by a pharmacist
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Self-medication, sharing prescriptions, taking overdoses, or failing to complete prescribed antibiotic courses are forms of drug misuse/abuse.

26. In Nigeria, which two federal agencies are respectively responsible for (i) regulating the manufacture and safety of food, drugs, and cosmetics, and (ii) combating illicit hard drug trafficking and abuse?
- A) NAFDAC and NDLEA
- B) FRSC and NEMA
- C) INEC and EFCC
- D) SON and ICPC
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: NAFDAC (National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control) regulates food/drug quality, while NDLEA (National Drug Law Enforcement Agency) combats illicit narcotics.

weeks.detectedHeading: Week 10: Reproductive System — Male and Female Reproductive Organs and Fertilization
weeks.lessonTitle: Reproductive System — Male and Female Reproductive Organs and Fertilization
weeks.content:
The male reproductive system includes the testes (held in the scrotal sac to maintain a temperature slightly below body temperature for sperm production), epididymis, vas deferens (sperm duct), seminal vesicles, prostate gland, and penis/urethra.
The female reproductive system includes the ovaries (produce ova/eggs and female sex hormones), fallopian tubes/oviducts (the exact site where fertilization occurs), uterus/womb (where the implanted embryo/foetus develops), cervix, and vagina (birth canal).

27. In which specific organ of the human female reproductive system does fertilization (fusion of the male sperm nucleus and female ovum nucleus) normally take place?
- A) Fallopian tube (oviduct)
- B) Uterus (womb)
- C) Ovary
- D) Cervix
Correct Answer: A
Explanation: Fertilization takes place in the upper part of the fallopian tube (oviduct), after which the zygote travels to the uterus for implantation.

passages.sectionHeading: Week 2: Living and Non-Living Things II — Characteristics of Living Things (MR NIGER D) and Classification of Living Things
passages.lessonTitle: Living and Non-Living Things II — Characteristics of Living Things (MR NIGER D) and Classification of Living Things
passages.content:
5. Which life process involves the chemical breakdown of food substances (glucose) inside living cells to release energy for metabolic activities? A) Respiration B) Excretion C) Egestion D) Transpiration
6. Why is the removal of undigested food faeces through the anus called egestion rather than excretion? A) Undigested faeces were never absorbed into body cells or formed by cellular metabolism, whereas excretion removes metabolic waste like urea, sweat, and carbon dioxide B) Egestion occurs only in green plants, whereas excretion occurs only in vertebrates C) Egestion takes place in the kidneys and lungs, whereas excretion takes place in the large intestine D) Egestion produces metabolic energy, whereas excretion stores excess glucose
7. How does nutrition in green plants (autotrophic nutrition) differ fundamentally from nutrition in animals (heterotrophic nutrition)? A) Green plants manufacture their own organic food from carbon dioxide and water using sunlight and chlorophyll, whereas animals depend on ready-made organic food B) Green plants feed only on dead decaying animals, whereas animals synthesize starch in chloroplasts C) Green plants respire only during the day, whereas animals photosynthesize at night D) Green plants lack cellular membranes, whereas animals possess rigid cellulose cell walls
keyFacts: @@MCQ@@{"questionNumber":5,"stem":"Which life process involves the chemical breakdown of food substances (glucose) inside living cells to release energy for metabolic activities?","options":["Respiration","Excretion","Egestion","Transpiration"],"correctOptionId":"A","explanation":"Cellular respiration breaks down glucose to release usable energy (ATP), whereas breathing is merely gaseous exchange."}

@@MCQ@@{"questionNumber":6,"stem":"Why is the removal of undigested food faeces through the anus called egestion rather than excretion?","options":["Undigested faeces were never absorbed into body cells or formed by cellular metabolism, whereas excretion removes metabolic waste like urea, sweat, and carbon dioxide","Egestion occurs only in green plants, whereas excretion occurs only in vertebrates","Egestion takes place in the kidneys and lungs, whereas excretion takes place in the large intestine","Egestion produces metabolic energy, whereas excretion stores excess glucose"],"correctOptionId":"A","explanation":"Excretion is strictly the removal of toxic waste products of cellular metabolism (urea, $\\text{CO}_2$, excess salts), whereas egestion expels undigested food residue."}

@@MCQ@@{"questionNumber":7,"stem":"How does nutrition in green plants (autotrophic nutrition) differ fundamentally from nutrition in animals (heterotrophic nutrition)?","options":["Green plants manufacture their own organic food from carbon dioxide and water using sunlight and chlorophyll, whereas animals depend on ready-made organic food","Green plants feed only on dead decaying animals, whereas animals synthesize starch in chloroplasts","Green plants respire only during the day, whereas animals photosynthesize at night","Green plants lack cellular membranes, whereas animals possess rigid cellulose cell walls"],"correctOptionId":"A","explanation":"Green plants are autotrophs that carry out photosynthesis using chlorophyll and sunlight, while animals are heterotrophs."}

passages.subject: Basic Science
passages.sectionHeading: Week 3: Living and Non-Living Things III — Plant and Animal Cells, Organelles, and Differences Between Plants and Animals
passages.lessonTitle: Living and Non-Living Things III — Plant and Animal Cells, Organelles, and Differences Between Plants and Animals
passages.content:
8. Which two structures are present in a typical green leaf palisade cell (plant cell) but completely absent in a human cheek cell (animal cell)? A) Rigid cellulose cell wall and chloroplasts B) Nucleus and selectively permeable cell membrane C) Mitochondria and cytoplasm D) Ribosomes and nuclear membrane
9. Which cell organelle is known as the "powerhouse of the cell" because it serves as the site of cellular respiration and energy (ATP) generation? A) Mitochondrion B) Chloroplast C) Golgi apparatus D) Vacuole
10. In what chemical form do green plants store excess carbohydrates compared to the storage form in animals and fungi? A) Plants store carbohydrates as insoluble starch granules, whereas animals store carbohydrates as glycogen in the liver and muscles B) Plants store carbohydrates as glycogen, whereas animals store carbohydrates as cellulose C) Plants store carbohydrates as urea, whereas animals store carbohydrates as chlorophyll D) Both plants and animals store carbohydrates exclusively as sucrose crystals

@@MCQ@@{"questionNumber":10,"stem":"In what chemical form do green plants store excess carbohydrates compared to the storage form in animals and fungi?","options":["Plants store carbohydrates as insoluble starch granules, whereas animals store carbohydrates as glycogen in the liver and muscles","Plants store carbohydrates as glycogen, whereas animals store carbohydrates as cellulose","Plants store carbohydrates as urea, whereas animals store carbohydrates as chlorophyll","Both plants and animals store carbohydrates exclusively as sucrose crystals"],"correctOptionId":"A","explanation":"Plants store excess glucose as starch, whereas animals store excess glucose as glycogen."}

passages.subject: Basic Science
passages.sectionHeading: Week 4: Living and Non-Living Things IV — Classification of Non-Living Things into Metals and Non-Metals
passages.lessonTitle: Living and Non-Living Things IV — Classification of Non-Living Things into Metals and Non-Metals
passages.content:
11. Which physical property of copper and aluminium enables them to be drawn into long, thin electrical transmission wires without snapping? A) Ductility B) Malleability C) Sonorousness D) Brittleness
12. Which of the following pairs correctly identifies a metal and a non-metal that exist as liquids at ordinary room temperature ($25^\circ\text{C}$)? A) Mercury (liquid metal) and Bromine (liquid non-metal) B) Iron (liquid metal) and Sulphur (liquid non-metal) C) Copper (liquid metal) and Carbon (liquid non-metal) D) Aluminium (liquid metal) and Iodine (liquid non-metal)
13. How do metal atoms and non-metal atoms behave differently with respect to valence electrons during ionic chemical reactions? A) Metal atoms lose electrons to form positively charged cations, whereas non-metal atoms gain electrons to form negatively charged anions B) Metal atoms gain electrons to form negative anions, whereas non-metal atoms lose electrons to form positive cations C) Both metal and non-metal atoms lose protons from their atomic nuclei D) Metal atoms share neutrons, whereas non-metal atoms destroy valence shells
14. Which atypical form of the non-metal carbon is a good conductor of electricity and is used as electrodes in dry cells? A) Graphite B) Diamond C) Sulphur D) Phosphorus

@@MCQ@@{"questionNumber":12,"stem":"Which of the following pairs correctly identifies a metal and a non-metal that exist as liquids at ordinary room temperature ($25^\\circ\\text{C}$)?","options":["Mercury (liquid metal) and Bromine (liquid non-metal)","Iron (liquid metal) and Sulphur (liquid non-metal)","Copper (liquid metal) and Carbon (liquid non-metal)","Aluminium (liquid metal) and Iodine (liquid non-metal)"],"correctOptionId":"A","explanation":"Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature, and bromine is the only non-metal that is liquid at room temperature."}

@@MCQ@@{"questionNumber":13,"stem":"How do metal atoms and non-metal atoms behave differently with respect to valence electrons during ionic chemical reactions?","options":["Metal atoms lose electrons to form positively charged cations, whereas non-metal atoms gain electrons to form negatively charged anions","Metal atoms gain electrons to form negative anions, whereas non-metal atoms lose electrons to form positive cations","Both metal and non-metal atoms lose protons from their atomic nuclei","Metal atoms share neutrons, whereas non-metal atoms destroy valence shells"],"correctOptionId":"A","explanation":"Metals are electropositive (losing electrons to form cations), whereas non-metals are electronegative (gaining electrons to form anions)."}

passages.subject: Basic Science
passages.sectionHeading: Week 5: Human Development — Growth, Developmental Changes, and Puberty in Boys and Girls
passages.lessonTitle: Human Development — Growth, Developmental Changes, and Puberty in Boys and Girls
passages.content:
15. Which hormone is secreted by the testes to trigger secondary sexual characteristics such as deepening of the voice and facial hair growth in boys at puberty? A) Testosterone B) Oestrogen C) Progesterone D) Insulin
16. Which of the following developmental changes at puberty occurs in BOTH boys and girls? A) Growth of pubic and armpit (axillary) hair and increased activity of sweat and sebaceous glands B) Onset of monthly menstruation (menarche) and widening of the pelvic girdle C) Enlargement of the larynx (Adam's apple) and production of sperm cells D) Development of mammary glands (breasts) and ovulation
17. Which statement accurately distinguishes temporary changes from permanent changes in human development? A) Sweating, pimples, and temporary weight fluctuations are reversible temporary changes, whereas growth in skeletal height and transition from infancy to adulthood are irreversible permanent changes B) Growing taller from childhood to adulthood is a temporary change, whereas sweating after exercise is a permanent change C) Chameleon skin colour change is a permanent change, whereas greying of hair in old age is a temporary change D) Both skeletal height growth and emotional moods are easily reversed at will

passages.subject: Basic Science
passages.sectionHeading: Week 6: Family Health I — Personal Cleanliness, Environmental Sanitation, Refuse Disposal, and Sewage Disposal
passages.lessonTitle: Family Health I — Personal Cleanliness, Environmental Sanitation, Refuse Disposal, and Sewage Disposal
passages.content:
18. What is the precise distinction between "refuse" and "sewage" in environmental sanitation? A) Refuse consists of solid dry waste materials (such as paper, tins, plastics, and food peels), whereas sewage consists of liquid wastewater and human excreta (urine and faeces) B) Refuse is flushed through underground water pipes, whereas sewage is burned in open incinerators C) Refuse contains only liquid industrial chemicals, whereas sewage contains only dry fallen leaves D) Refuse is disposed of in septic tanks, whereas sewage is recycled into plastic bottles
19. Which method of refuse disposal decomposes biodegradable organic waste (such as vegetable peels and plant leaves) through microbial action to produce nutrient-rich farm manure? A) Composting B) Incineration C) Open dumping D) Pulverization of plastics
20. Why must non-biodegradable refuse such as plastic bottles, polythene bags, and glass jars be separated from compost pits? A) Microorganisms cannot decompose non-biodegradable materials, so they persist in soil and cause long-term land pollution B) Non-biodegradable plastics dissolve instantly in rainwater to form nitrogen fertilizer C) Non-biodegradable glass evaporates into the atmosphere at room temperature D) Soil earthworms consume glass and polythene as their primary source of protein
keyFacts: @@MCQ@@{"questionNumber":18,"stem":"What is the precise distinction between \"refuse\" and \"sewage\" in environmental sanitation?","options":["Refuse consists of solid dry waste materials (such as paper, tins, plastics, and food peels), whereas sewage consists of liquid wastewater and human excreta (urine and faeces)","Refuse is flushed through underground water pipes, whereas sewage is burned in open incinerators","Refuse contains only liquid industrial chemicals, whereas sewage contains only dry fallen leaves","Refuse is disposed of in septic tanks, whereas sewage is recycled into plastic bottles"],"correctOptionId":"A","explanation":"Refuse is solid waste, while sewage is liquid waste containing human excreta and domestic/industrial wastewater."}

@@MCQ@@{"questionNumber":19,"stem":"Which method of refuse disposal decomposes biodegradable organic waste (such as vegetable peels and plant leaves) through microbial action to produce nutrient-rich farm manure?","options":["Composting","Incineration","Open dumping","Pulverization of plastics"],"correctOptionId":"A","explanation":"Composting biologically decomposes organic biodegradable refuse into rich humus fertilizer."}

@@MCQ@@{"questionNumber":20,"stem":"Why must non-biodegradable refuse such as plastic bottles, polythene bags, and glass jars be separated from compost pits?","options":["Microorganisms cannot decompose non-biodegradable materials, so they persist in soil and cause long-term land pollution","Non-biodegradable plastics dissolve instantly in rainwater to form nitrogen fertilizer","Non-biodegradable glass evaporates into the atmosphere at room temperature","Soil earthworms consume glass and polythene as their primary source of protein"],"correctOptionId":"A","explanation":"Non-biodegradable materials cannot be broken down by natural decomposers (bacteria and fungi) and must be recycled or reused instead."}

passages.sectionHeading: Week 8: Family Health II — Nutrition, Classes of Food, and Balanced Diet
passages.lessonTitle: Family Health II — Nutrition, Classes of Food, and Balanced Diet
passages.content:
21. A young child fed almost exclusively on starchy pap and cassava develops a swollen pot-belly, thin wasted limbs, oedema, and reddish-brown scanty hair. Which nutritional deficiency disease is this? A) Kwashiorkor (severe protein deficiency) B) Scurvy (Vitamin C deficiency) C) Goitre (Iodine deficiency) D) Rickets (Vitamin D and Calcium deficiency)
22. Which pair correctly matches a specific vitamin with the deficiency condition caused by its absence in the human diet? A) Vitamin C — Scurvy (bleeding gums and poor wound healing); Vitamin D — Rickets (soft, bowed bones) B) Vitamin A — Beriberi; Vitamin K — Night blindness C) Vitamin B1 — Rickets; Vitamin C — Failure of blood to clot D) Vitamin D — Bleeding gums; Vitamin A — Goitre
23. Which mineral element is an essential component of haemoglobin in red blood cells, and which mineral element prevents enlargement of the thyroid gland (goitre)? A) Iron (for haemoglobin) and Iodine (to prevent goitre) B) Sodium (for haemoglobin) and Potassium (to prevent goitre) C) Calcium (for haemoglobin) and Fluorine (to prevent goitre) D) Magnesium (for haemoglobin) and Chlorine (to prevent goitre)
24. Which chemical reagents are used in the laboratory to test for the presence of Starch and Simple Reducing Sugar (Glucose) respectively? A) Iodine solution (turns blue-black with starch) and Fehling's or Benedict's solution (turns brick-red precipitate on heating with glucose) B) Million's reagent (for starch) and Sudan III solution (for glucose) C) Litmus paper (for starch) and limewater (for glucose) D) Biuret reagent (for starch) and translucent paper mark (for glucose)

@@MCQ@@{"questionNumber":23,"stem":"Which mineral element is an essential component of haemoglobin in red blood cells, and which mineral element prevents enlargement of the thyroid gland (goitre)?","options":["Iron (for haemoglobin) and Iodine (to prevent goitre)","Sodium (for haemoglobin) and Potassium (to prevent goitre)","Calcium (for haemoglobin) and Fluorine (to prevent goitre)","Magnesium (for haemoglobin) and Chlorine (to prevent goitre)"],"correctOptionId":"A","explanation":"Iron is required to synthesize oxygen-carrying haemoglobin (deficiency causes anaemia), while iodine is required by the thyroid gland to synthesize thyroxine (deficiency causes goitre)."}

passages.lessonTitle: Family Health III — Drug and Substance Abuse
passages.content:
25. Which of the following practices constitutes drug abuse even when using a legal pharmaceutical medicine? A) Self-medicating with antibiotics without a doctor's prescription or stopping the dosage before completing the prescribed course B) Taking the exact dosage of antimalarial tablets prescribed by a licensed physician at the recommended intervals C) Checking the NAFDAC registration number and expiry date before purchasing a medicine from a registered pharmacy D) Storing prescribed liquid medicines out of the reach of toddlers as instructed by a pharmacist
26. In Nigeria, which two federal agencies are respectively responsible for (i) regulating the manufacture and safety of food, drugs, and cosmetics, and (ii) combating illicit hard drug trafficking and abuse? A) NAFDAC and NDLEA B) FRSC and NEMA C) INEC and EFCC D) SON and ICPC

passages.subject: Basic Science
passages.sectionHeading: Week 10: Reproductive System — Male and Female Reproductive Organs and Fertilization
passages.lessonTitle: Reproductive System — Male and Female Reproductive Organs and Fertilization
passages.content:
27. In which specific organ of the human female reproductive system does fertilization (fusion of the male sperm nucleus and female ovum nucleus) normally take place? A) Fallopian tube (oviduct) B) Uterus (womb) C) Ovary D) Cervix
28. Why are the human testes suspended outside the abdominal cavity inside the scrotal sac? A) Healthy sperm production (spermatogenesis) requires a temperature $2^\circ\text{C}$ to $3^\circ\text{C}$ lower than normal core body temperature ($37^\circ\text{C}$) B) The abdominal cavity lacks blood vessels to supply oxygen to the testes C) The scrotal sac heats the testes to $42^\circ\text{C}$ to accelerate hormone breakdown D) Sperm cells are produced in the kidneys and only pass through the scrotum during urination

passages.sectionHeading: Week 11: Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs), HIV/AIDS, Modes of Transmission, and Prevention
passages.lessonTitle: Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs), HIV/AIDS, Modes of Transmission, and Prevention
passages.content:
29. How does the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) cause Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS) in an infected person? A) It progressively attacks and destroys the body's CD4 helper T-lymphocytes (white blood cells), leaving the body defenseless against opportunistic infections B) It multiplies inside red blood cells to increase oxygen transport in the bloodstream C) It strengthens bone marrow platelets so that blood clots inside the digestive tract D) It converts liver glycogen into excess insulin within twenty-four hours of exposure
30. Which of the following CANNOT transmit HIV from an infected person to a healthy person? A) Sharing classroom desks, shaking hands, hugging, or being bitten by mosquitoes B) Receiving a blood transfusion of unscreened HIV-positive blood C) Sharing unsterilized hypodermic needles, razor blades, or tattooing instruments D) Mother-to-child transmission during childbirth or breastfeeding without antiretroviral care
